In [[probability theory]], the '''van den Berg–Kesten (BK) inequality''' or '''van den Berg–Kesten–Reimer (BKR) inequality''' states that the probability for two [[Event (probability theory)|random events]] to both happen, and at the same time one can find "disjoint certificates" to show that they both happen, is at most the product of their individual probabilities. The special case for two monotone events (the notion as used in the [[FKG inequality]]) was first proved by van den Berg and [[Harry Kesten|Kesten]]<ref name = "BK">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1017/s0021900200029326| issn = 0021-9002| volume = 22| issue = 3| pages = 556–569| last1 = van den Berg| first1 = J.| last2 = Kesten| first2 = H.|author2-link = Harry Kesten | title = Inequalities with applications to percolation and reliability| journal = [[Journal of Applied Probability]]| date = 1985|mr = 799280|url = https://dx.doi.org/10.1017/s0021900200029326|via = [[The Wikipedia Library]]| url-access = subscription}}</ref> in 1985, who also conjectured that the inequality holds in general, not requiring monotonicity. {{ill|David Reimer (mathematician)|lt=Reimer|fr|David Reimer (mathématicien)|de|David Reimer (Mathematiker)
}}<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1017/S0963548399004113| issn = 0963-5483| volume = 9| issue = 1| pages = 27–32| last = Reimer| first = David| title = Proof of the Van den Berg–Kesten Conjecture| journal = [[Combinatorics, Probability and Computing]] | date = 2000|mr = 1751301| s2cid = 33118560|url = https://dx.doi.org/10.1017/S0963548399004113|via = The Wikipedia Library| url-access = subscription}}</ref> later proved this conjecture.<ref name = "review">{{Cite book| publisher = Birkhäuser| isbn = 978-1-4612-2168-5| pages = 159–173| editor1-first = Maury|editor1-last =  Bramson |editor2-first =  Rick|editor2-last = Durrett| last1 = Borgs| first1 = Christian| last2 = Chayes| first2 = Jennifer T.| last3 = Randall| first3 = Dana| title = Perplexing Problems in Probability: Festschrift in Honor of Harry Kesten| chapter = The van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer Inequality: A Review| location = Boston, MA| series = Progress in Probability| date = 1999| doi = 10.1007/978-1-4612-2168-5_9 |chapter-url = https://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-2168-5_9 |via = The Wikipedia Library|mr = 1703130}}</ref>{{rp|159}}<ref name = "bollobas">{{Cite book| first1 = Béla |last1 = Bollobás|author1-link = Béla Bollobás|first2 = Oliver |last2 = Riordan|author2-link = Oliver Riordan|chapter = 2 - Probabilistic tools |title = Percolation| doi = 10.1017/CBO9781139167383.003|year = 2006 | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | pages = 36–49 | isbn=9780521872324 |url = https://dx.doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139167383.003 |via = The Wikipedia Library|mr = 2283880}}</ref>{{rp|44}} The inequality is applied to probability spaces with a [[product measure|product structure]], such as in [[percolation]] problems.<ref>{{cite journal|first1 = Geoffrey R.|last1 = Grimmett|author1-link = Geoffrey Grimmett|first2 = Gregory F. |last2 = Lawler|author2-link = Greg Lawler|title = Harry Kesten (1931–2019): A Personal and Scientific Tribute| journal = [[Notices of the AMS]]|doi = 10.1090/noti2100|pages = 822–831|year = 2020|volume = 67 | number = 6| s2cid=210164713 |quote = The highly novel BK (van den Berg/Kesten) inequality plays a key role in systems subjected to a product measure such as percolation.|doi-access = free|arxiv = 2001.03639}}</ref>{{rp|829}}

== Statement ==
Let <math>\Omega_1, \Omega_2, \ldots, \Omega_n</math> be [[probability spaces]], each of finitely many elements. The inequality applies to spaces of the form <math>\Omega = \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \times \cdots \times \Omega_n</math>, equipped with the [[product measure]], so that each element <math>x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \Omega</math> is given the probability
<math display = "block"> \mathbb P(\{x\}) = \mathbb P_1(\{x_1\}) \cdots \mathbb P_n(\{x_n\}).</math>

For two events <math>A, B\subseteq \Omega</math>, their ''disjoint occurrence'' <math>A \mathbin{\square} B</math> is defined as the event consisting of configurations <math>x</math> whose memberships in <math>A</math> and in <math>B</math> can be verified on disjoint subsets of indices. Formally, <math>x \in A \mathbin{\square} B</math> if there exist subsets <math>I, J \subseteq [n]</math> such that:
# <math>I \cap J = \varnothing,</math>
# for all <math>y</math> that agrees with <math>x</math> on <math>I</math> (in other words, <math>y_i = x_i\  \forall i \in I</math>), <math>y</math> is also in <math>A,</math> and 
# similarly every <math>z</math> that agrees with <math>x</math> on <math>J</math> is in <math>B.</math>
The inequality asserts that:
<math display = "block"> \mathbb P (A \mathbin{\square} B) \le \mathbb P (A) \mathbb P (B)</math>
for every pair of events <math>A</math> and <math>B.</math><ref name = "review"/>{{rp|160}}

== Examples ==

=== Coin tosses ===
If <math>\Omega</math> corresponds to tossing a [[fair coin]] <math>n = 10</math> times, then each <math>\Omega_i = \{ H, T\}</math> consists of the two possible outcomes, heads or tails, with equal probability. Consider the event <math>A</math> that there exists 3 consecutive heads, and the event <math>B</math> that there are at least 5 heads in total. Then <math>A \mathbin \square B</math> would be the following event: there are 3 consecutive heads, and discarding those there are another 5 heads remaining. This event has probability at most <math> \mathbb P ( A) \mathbb P ( B),</math><ref name = "bollobas"/>{{rp|42}} which is to say the probability of getting <math>A</math> in 10 tosses, and getting <math>B</math> in another 10 tosses, [[independent (probability)|independent]] of each other.

Numerically, <math>\mathbb P ( A) = 520/1024 \approx 0.5078,</math><ref>{{WolframAlpha |title=3 consecutive heads in 10 coin flips |id=3+consecutive+heads+in+10+coin+flips }}</ref> <math>\mathbb P ( B) = 638/1024 \approx 0.6230,</math><ref>{{WolframAlpha |title=at least 5 heads in 10 coin flips|id=at+least+5+heads+in+10+coin+flips }}</ref> and their disjoint occurrence would imply at least 8 heads,<!-- in fact equal in this case but let's not get into this --> so <math>\mathbb P ( A\mathbin \square B) \le \mathbb P(\text{8 heads or more}) = 56/1024 \approx 0.0547.</math><ref>{{WolframAlpha |title=at least 8 heads in 10 coin flips|id=at+least+8+heads+in+10+coin+flips }}</ref><!-- [[WP:CALC]] of a concrete case of the cited example, which just says "It is hard not to be convinced ..." -->

=== Percolation ===

In (Bernoulli) [[bond percolation]] of a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]], the <math>\Omega_i</math>'s are indexed by edges. Each edge is kept (or "open") with some probability <math>p,</math> or otherwise removed (or "closed"), independent of other edges, and one studies questions about the connectivity of the remaining graph, for example the event <math>u \leftrightarrow v </math> that there is a path between two vertices <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> using only open edges. For events of such form, the disjoint occurrence <math>A \mathbin \square B</math> is the event where there exist two open paths not sharing any edges (corresponding to the subsets <math>I</math> and <math>J</math> in the definition), such that the first one providing the connection required by <math>A,</math> and the second for <math>B.</math><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1007/BF02180133| issn = 1572-9613| volume = 78| issue = 5| pages = 1311–1324| last = Grimmett| first = Geoffrey| title = Comparison and disjoint-occurrence inequalities for random-cluster models| journal = Journal of Statistical Physics| access-date = 2022-12-18| date = 1995-03-01| bibcode = 1995JSP....78.1311G| url = https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02180133 |mr = 1316106| s2cid = 16426885| url-access = subscription}}</ref>{{rp|1322}}<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI| volume = 6| pages = 53–66| last1 = Chayes| first1 = Jennifer Tour| last2 = Puha| first2 = Amber L.| last3 = Sweet| first3 = Ted| title = Probability theory and applications| chapter = Lecture 1. The Basics of Percolation (in ''Independent and dependent percolation'')| series = IAS/Park City Math. Ser.| access-date = 2022-12-18| date = 1999| mr = 1678308 |chapter-url = http://www.cts.cuni.cz/soubory/konference/pdf.pdf#page=17 }}</ref>

The inequality can be used to prove a version of the [[exponential decay]] phenomenon in the [[Percolation theory#Subcritical and supercritical|subcritical regime]], namely that on the [[integer lattice]] graph <math>\mathbb Z^d,</math> for <math> p < p_\mathrm c</math> a suitably defined [[Percolation threshold|critical probability]], the radius of the connected component containing the origin obeys a distribution with exponentially small tails:

<math display = "block>\mathbb P( 0 \leftrightarrow \partial [-r, r]^d) \le \exp(- c r) </math>
for some constant <math>c > 0</math> depending on <math>p.</math> Here <math>\partial [-r, r]^d</math> consists of vertices <math>x</math> that satisfies <math>\max_{1 \le i \le d} |x_i| = r.</math><ref>{{Cite book|first1 = Geoffrey R.|last1 = Grimmett| edition = 2| publisher = Cambridge University Press| isbn = 978-1-108-43817-9| pages = 86–130 | title = Probability on Graphs: Random Processes on Graphs and Lattices| chapter = 5.1 Subcritical Phase |url =  | location = Cambridge| series = Institute of Mathematical Statistics Textbooks| date = 2018| doi = 10.1017/9781108528986.006 |mr = 2723356 }}</ref>{{rp|87–90}}<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.4171/lem/62-1/2-12| issn = 0013-8584| volume = 62| issue = 1| pages = 199–206| last1 = Duminil-Copin| first1 = Hugo|author1-link = Hugo Duminil-Copin| last2 = Tassion| first2 = Vincent| title = A new proof of the sharpness of the phase transition for Bernoulli percolation on <math>\mathbb Z^d</math>| journal = L'Enseignement Mathématique | date = 2017-01-30| arxiv = 1502.03051| url = https://ems.press/journals/lem/articles/14583 |quote = The proof of Item 1 (with <math>\tilde p_c</math> in place of <math>p_c</math>) can be derived from the BK-inequality [vdBK].|mr = 3605816| s2cid = 119307436}}</ref>{{rp|202}}

== Extensions ==
=== Multiple events ===
When there are three or more events, the operator <math>\square</math> may not be [[associative]], because given a subset of indices <math>K</math> on which <math>x \in A \mathbin \square B</math> can be verified, it might not be possible to split <math>K</math> a disjoint union <math>I \sqcup J</math> such that <math>I</math> witnesses <math>x \in A</math> and <math>J</math> witnesses <math>x \in B</math>.<ref name = "bollobas"/>{{rp|43}} For example, there exists an event <math>A \subseteq \{0, 1\}^6</math> such that <math>\left((A \mathbin \square A) \mathbin \square A\right) \mathbin \square A \neq (A \mathbin \square A) \mathbin \square (A \mathbin \square A).</math><ref name = "infty">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.3150/16-BEJ883| issn = 1350-7265| volume = 24| issue = 1| pages = 433–448| last1 = Arratia| first1 = Richard|author-link1=Richard Arratia| last2 = Garibaldi| first2 = Skip|author-link2=Skip Garibaldi| last3 = Hales| first3 = Alfred W.|author-link3=Alfred W. Hales| title = The van den Berg–Kesten–Reimer operator and inequality for infinite spaces| journal = [[Bernoulli (journal)|Bernoulli]] | date = 2018|mr = 3706764| s2cid = 4666324| doi-access = free| arxiv = 1508.05337}}</ref>{{rp|447}}

Nonetheless, one can define the <math>k</math>-ary BKR operation of events <math>A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k</math> as the set of configurations <math>x</math> where there are pairwise disjoint subset of indices <math>I_i \subseteq [n]</math> such that <math>I_i</math> witnesses the membership of <math>x</math> in <math>A_i.</math> This operation satisfies:
<math display = "block"> A_1 \mathbin \square A_2 \mathbin \square A_3 \mathbin \square \cdots \mathbin \square A_k \subseteq \left( \cdots \left((A_1 \mathbin \square A_2) \mathbin \square A_3 \right) \mathbin \square \cdots \right) \mathbin \square A_k,</math>
whence 
<math display = "block">\begin{align} 
\mathbb P( A_1 \mathbin \square A_2 \mathbin \square A_3 \mathbin \square \cdots \mathbin \square A_k) &\le \mathbb P\left(
 \left( \cdots \left((A_1 \mathbin \square A_2) \mathbin \square A_3 \right) \mathbin \square \cdots \right) \mathbin \square A_k\right) \\
&\le \mathbb P( A_1) \mathbb P( A_2) \cdots \mathbb P( A_k)
\end{align}
</math>
by repeated use of the original BK inequality.<ref name = "implausilucky"/>{{rp|204–205}} This inequality was one factor used to analyse the winner statistics from the [[Florida Lottery]] and identify  what ''[[Mathematics Magazine]]'' referred to as "implausibly lucky"<ref name = "implausilucky"/>{{rp|210}} individuals, confirmed later by enforcement investigation<ref>{{Cite web| title = Math used in Post's Florida Lottery investigation published in journal| work = [[Palm Beach Post]]| access-date = 2022-12-18|date = 2015-07-15| url = https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/local/2015/07/15/math-used-in-post-s/7571402007/ |first = Lawrence |last = Mower| archive-date = 2022-12-18| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20221218231404/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/local/2015/07/15/math-used-in-post-s/7571402007/|quote = Some of the frequent winners, including the top one, were part of an underground market for winning lottery tickets, lottery investigators later found.}}</ref> that law violations were involved.<ref name = "implausilucky">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.4169/math.mag.88.3.196| issn = 0025-570X| volume = 88| issue = 3| pages = 196–211| last1 = Arratia| first1 = Richard| last2 = Garibaldi| first2 = Skip| last3 = Mower| first3 = Lawrence| last4 = Stark| first4 = Philip B.| title = Some People Have All the Luck| journal = [[Mathematics Magazine]]| access-date = 2022-12-18| date = 2015-06-01| arxiv = 1503.02902| url = https://doi.org/10.4169/math.mag.88.3.196 |mr = 3383910| s2cid = 15631424}}</ref>{{rp|210}}

=== Spaces of larger cardinality ===
When <math>\Omega_i</math> is allowed to be infinite, measure theoretic issues arise. For <math>\Omega = [0, 1]^n</math> and <math>\mathbb P</math> the [[Lebesgue measure]], there are measurable subsets <math>A, B \subseteq \Omega</math> such that <math>A \mathbin \square B</math> is [[non-measurable]] (so <math>\mathbb P(A \mathbin \square B)</math> in the inequality is not defined),<ref name = "infty"/>{{rp|437}} but the following theorem still holds:<ref name = "infty"/>{{rp|440}}
<blockquote>
If <math>A, B \subseteq [0, 1]^n</math> are Lebesgue measurable, then there is some [[Borel set]] <math>C</math> such that:
* <math>A \mathbin \square B \subseteq C,</math> and
* <math>\mathbb P(C) \le \mathbb P(A) \mathbb P(B).</math>
</blockquote>
